reference_answer: When search is LIMITED to depth d, if an UNAVOIDABLE 'DISASTER' (e.g. LOSING a valuable piece) will occur at depth d+3 (BEYOND the search 'HORIZON'), the program can be 'FOOLED' by DELAYING moves (e.g. 'check' moves or threats that are NOT REALLY dangerous) aimed at 'PUSHING' the disaster's timing FURTHER beyond the horizon (no longer WITHIN the d-step range being considered) — this causes the evaluation function at depth d to 'SEE' a state that LOOKS 'SAFE' (since the disaster has NOT YET occurred WITHIN the examined range), while in REALITY it is only 'DELAYING' the INEVITABLE (usually at an EVEN HIGHER cost) — a PARTIAL SOLUTION: 'QUIESCENCE SEARCH' — extending the search FURTHER at 'UNSTABLE' nodes (e.g. currently in a piece EXCHANGE/check) BEYOND the NORMAL depth limit until reaching a MORE 'QUIET' state for a MORE ACCURATE evaluation.
key_points: Horizon Effect: when search is limited to depth d, if an unavoidable disaster occurs at depth d+3, the program can be fooled by delaying moves that push the disaster's timing beyond the d-step range being considered

The evaluation function at depth d sees a state that looks safe though it's really just delaying the inevitable (usually at a higher cost); a partial solution is Quiescence Search — extending the search further at unstable nodes until reaching a more quiet state

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Why High Test-Set Accuracy Alone May Not Be Trustworthy Without Interpretability
question: In HIGH-STAKES domains (e.g. healthcare, finance, justice), analyze why achieving HIGH Accuracy on the test set ALONE is NOT sufficient for a model to be TRUSTED for deployment, and the role of Interpretability/Explainability.
reference_answer: Test-set Accuracy only measures AVERAGE performance on a FINITE sample, and does NOT guarantee the model learned the CORRECT 'REASONS' (the TRUE underlying causes) — a model COULD achieve HIGH Accuracy by 'ROTE LEARNING' SPURIOUS CORRELATIONS that just HAPPEN to hold in the COLLECTED dataset (e.g. a disease-diagnosis model from X-ray images 'LEARNS' to distinguish based on the SCANNING MACHINE'S label at different hospitals instead of the TRUE PATHOLOGICAL signs, if data from different hospitals has SYSTEMATICALLY different patient ratios) — in HIGH-STAKES domains, UNDERSTANDING 'WHY' a model made a SPECIFIC decision (via techniques like SHAP, LIME, or using inherently INTERPRETABLE models) helps DETECT such SPURIOUS correlations EARLY, allowing human EXPERTS to VERIFY the REASONABLENESS of the reasoning before FULLY TRUSTING a prediction, especially in 'EDGE' or ANOMALOUS cases that OVERALL Accuracy does NOT fully capture.
key_points: Test-set Accuracy only measures average performance on a finite sample, not guaranteeing the model learned the true underlying reasons — it may rote-learn spurious correlations that just happen to hold in the collected data (e.g. learning by scanning-machine label instead of true pathology)

In high-stakes domains, interpretability (SHAP, LIME, or inherently interpretable models) helps detect spurious correlations early, letting experts verify reasoning before trusting predictions, especially in edge cases overall Accuracy doesn't capture

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Premature Convergence in Genetic Algorithms and How to Fix It
question: Analyze the phenomenon of 'Premature Convergence' in a Genetic Algorithm — when the population LOSES DIVERSITY and CONVERGES to a solution that is only good LOCALLY before adequately exploring the search space — and techniques to FIX it.
reference_answer: Premature convergence occurs when ONE (or a SMALL group of) individual(s) has fitness MUCH HIGHER than the REST of the population at an EARLY stage — because of the selection MECHANISM being PROPORTIONAL to fitness, this individual (and its OFFSPRING) quickly 'DOMINATES' the population, causing GENETIC DIVERSITY to DROP SHARPLY, and the population CONVERGES to the REGION near that individual — IF this is only a LOCAL (not global) optimum, the algorithm LOSES the ability to EXPLORE OTHER regions of the search space — FIXES: (1) INCREASE the mutation rate to maintain diversity; (2) use a 'SOFTER' selection mechanism (like rank-based instead of directly proportional to fitness, avoiding one TOO DOMINANT individual taking over IMMEDIATELY); (3) 'NICHING'/'SPECIATION' techniques — DIVIDING the population into subgroups exploring DIFFERENT regions, MAINTAINING diversity BETWEEN groups.
key_points: Premature convergence occurs when an individual with much higher fitness quickly dominates the population via proportional selection, causing genetic diversity to drop sharply and the population to converge to one region (possibly just a local optimum)

Fixes include increasing the mutation rate, using a softer selection mechanism (rank-based instead of directly proportional), or niching/speciation techniques dividing the population into subgroups exploring different regions to maintain diversity

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Min-Conflicts - Local Search Applied to CSP
question: How does the 'Min-Conflicts' algorithm (a form of Local Search applied to CSP) FUNDAMENTALLY differ from Backtracking Search, and why is it usually MUCH MORE EFFICIENT for VERY LARGE-scale CSP problems (e.g. scheduling with thousands of variables)?
reference_answer: Backtracking BUILDS a solution STEP BY STEP (assigning UNASSIGNED variables, backtracking on CONFLICT) — Min-Conflicts STARTS with a COMPLETE assignment (RANDOM or heuristic-based) for ALL variables (which MAY VIOLATE many constraints), then REPEATS: RANDOMLY choose a variable CURRENTLY VIOLATING a constraint, change its value to the one causing the FEWEST CONFLICTS (min-conflicts) with OTHER variables — stopping when there are NO more conflicts (a solution) or a MAXIMUM number of iterations is reached — being a form of LOCAL SEARCH (not REBUILDING from SCRATCH each time), it avoids having to 're-EXPLORE' the ENTIRE space FROM the root as Backtracking does — in PRACTICE, for STRUCTURED problems (like extremely large N-Queens scheduling), Min-Conflicts can find a solution in NEARLY CONSTANT time, while PLAIN Backtracking can TAKE a very long time due to having to BACKTRACK DEEPLY many times.
key_points: Backtracking builds a solution step by step (assigning unassigned variables, backtracking on conflict); Min-Conflicts starts with a complete assignment (possibly violating constraints), then repeatedly changes a violating variable's value to the one causing fewest conflicts

Being local search avoids re-exploring the entire space from the root; for large structured problems, Min-Conflicts can find a solution in nearly constant time while plain Backtracking can take very long due to deep backtracking

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The 'No Free Lunch' Theorem and Its Practical Implications
question: What does the 'No Free Lunch Theorem' (for Optimization/Machine Learning) state, and why does it imply that there is NO 'UNIVERSALLY BEST' machine learning algorithm for EVERY problem?
reference_answer: The theorem (stated at a GENERAL level) claims that: when AVERAGING performance over ALL POSSIBLE problems (with NO ASSUMPTIONS/constraints about problem STRUCTURE), EVERY optimization/machine-learning algorithm has EQUAL AVERAGE performance — consequence: an algorithm that performs WELL on a SPECIFIC class of problems (thanks to assumptions/inductive bias SUITED to the STRUCTURE of that class, e.g. a CNN assuming LOCALITY and translation invariance SUITED to IMAGES) MUST perform WORSE on SOME OTHER class of problems (where that assumption is NO LONGER TRUE) — PRACTICAL IMPLICATION: choosing an appropriate algorithm/architecture ALWAYS requires UNDERSTANDING the SPECIFIC STRUCTURE of the PARTICULAR problem being solved, there is NO 'UNIVERSAL FORMULA' that works WELL for EVERY situation — this is why 'DESIGNING features/architecture SUITED to the problem DOMAIN' REMAINS IMPORTANT even with Deep Learning.
key_points: No Free Lunch Theorem: when averaging over all possible problems (no structural assumptions), every optimization/ML algorithm has equal average performance

Consequence: an algorithm good on a specific problem class (thanks to inductive bias suited to it, e.g. CNN with images) must perform worse on some other class — need to understand problem structure to choose an algorithm, no universal formula

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing the Class Imbalance Problem and the SMOTE Technique
question: For a fraud detection problem (the 'fraud' class is only 0.1% of the data), analyze why training DIRECTLY on this SEVERELY imbalanced data usually gives a POOR model, and how the SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) technique fixes this.
reference_answer: With EXTREMELY imbalanced data, the OVERALL loss function is 'DOMINATED' by the MAJORITY class (misclassifying a MINORITY sample contributes NEGLIGIBLY to the total loss compared to OPTIMIZING for the MAJORITY class), causing the model to TEND to 'IGNORE' the MINORITY class ALMOST ENTIRELY (predicting EVERY sample as the majority class still achieves HIGH Accuracy but is USELESS for the TRUE PURPOSE — detecting fraud) — SMOTE fixes this by CREATING new 'SYNTHETIC' samples for the MINORITY class: for EACH minority sample, FIND a few 'NEAREST NEIGHBORS' (within the SAME minority class), then CREATE a NEW sample by RANDOM INTERPOLATION BETWEEN the original sample and that neighbor (instead of simply COPYING the old sample identically, INCREASING DIVERSITY rather than just repeating) — REBALANCING the class ratio in the TRAINING data, helping the model 'PAY MORE ATTENTION' to the CHARACTERISTICS of the minority class.
key_points: With extremely imbalanced data, the overall loss is dominated by the majority class, causing the model to nearly ignore the minority class (high Accuracy by always predicting majority, but useless for the true purpose like fraud detection)

SMOTE creates new synthetic minority samples by random interpolation between an original sample and its nearest same-class neighbor (not simple copying), rebalancing the training class ratio so the model pays more attention to minority-class characteristics

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: When a neural network already trained WELL on Task A is then trained FURTHER on Task B (WITHOUT reusing Task A's data), 'Catastrophic Forgetting' usually occurs — analyze the CAUSE and one direction for a fix.
reference_answer: A neural network's weights STORE 'KNOWLEDGE' of Task A in a DISTRIBUTED way (not CLEARLY SEPARATED into distinct parts per task) — when continuing to train (Gradient Descent) ON Task B, these weights get UPDATED in the direction OPTIMAL FOR Task B ALONE, with NO CONSTRAINT keeping IMPORTANT information for Task A — consequence: the network can 'FORGET' ALMOST COMPLETELY how to solve Task A even though it performed VERY WELL before — ONE fix direction: 'Elastic Weight Consolidation' (EWC) — after training on Task A, ESTIMATE how 'IMPORTANT' EACH weight IS FOR Task A (e.g. via the Fisher Information matrix), then when training on Task B, ADD a PENALTY term to the loss function to 'RESTRICT' those IMPORTANT weights from CHANGING TOO MUCH — allowing the network to LEARN the NEW task while still 'RETAINING' MOST of the OLD knowledge.
key_points: Network weights store knowledge distributed, not cleanly separated by task; continuing training on Task B updates weights optimally for B alone with no constraint preserving Task A's important information, causing near-total forgetting of A

Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC): estimate each weight's importance for Task A (e.g. via the Fisher matrix), then add a penalty when training on B restricting important weights from changing too much, retaining most old knowledge

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing the 'Hallucination' Phenomenon in Large Language Models
question: Analyze why Large Language Models can produce 'Hallucinations' (information that sounds CONFIDENT and FLUENT but is FACTUALLY WRONG or FABRICATED), and why this problem is HARD to fully fix just by INCREASING model/data size.
reference_answer: FUNDAMENTALLY, an LLM is trained to PREDICT the MOST LIKELY NEXT word based on the STATISTICAL PATTERNS of language it has learned, with NO EXPLICIT 'FACT-CHECKING' mechanism SEPARATE from the text-generation process — the model 'LEARNS' to generate text that SOUNDS 'LIKE' what commonly appears in the training data (including the STRUCTURE/STYLE of 'CONFIDENT' statements), but has NO 'GROUNDED UNDERSTANDING' of the REAL WORLD to RELIABLY DISTINGUISH between 'WHAT IS TRUE' and 'WHAT SOUNDS PLAUSIBLE BUT IS FALSE' — INCREASING model/data size can REDUCE hallucination frequency (since the model 'MEMORIZES'/generalizes MORE facts), but does NOT eliminate the UNDERLYING PROBLEM (the model can still ENCOUNTER questions BEYOND what it RELIABLY 'KNOWS', and will still 'CONFIDENTLY' ANSWER following statistical patterns instead of ADMITTING 'I DON'T KNOW') — ADDITIONAL techniques (like Retrieval-Augmented Generation, external fact-checking) are needed to FURTHER REDUCE this.
key_points: An LLM is trained to predict the most likely next word based on statistical language patterns, with no explicit fact-checking mechanism separate from text generation, so it can't reliably distinguish 'true' from 'sounds plausible but false'

Increasing model/data size reduces hallucination frequency but doesn't eliminate the underlying problem (the model still confidently answers beyond its reliable knowledge) — needs additional techniques like Retrieval-Augmented Generation, external fact-checking

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing Adversarial Examples and Their Implications for the Trustworthiness of Deep Learning Models
question: 'Adversarial Examples' — inputs altered by a VERY SMALL amount (usually IMPERCEPTIBLE to the naked eye for images) but causing a Deep Learning model to predict COMPLETELY WRONG with HIGH confidence — analyze why this phenomenon EXISTS, and its implications for deploying AI in HIGH-SAFETY applications (like self-driving cars).
reference_answer: A neural network learns an EXTREMELY COMPLEX 'DECISION BOUNDARY' in a HIGH-DIMENSIONAL input space — although this boundary CORRECTLY classifies most 'NATURAL' (real) data, it can be VERY 'CLOSE' to SOME data points along certain SPECIFIC DIRECTIONS in the HIGH-DIMENSIONAL space (even though those directions carry NO INTUITIVE MEANING to humans) — an attacker can COMPUTE (usually using the model's own GRADIENT) a VERY SMALL perturbation in EXACTLY that direction to 'PUSH' a data point ACROSS the decision boundary, while this CHANGE is TOO SMALL for the HUMAN EYE to notice (not affecting human PERCEPTION of the image) — this shows that a Deep Learning model's 'UNDERSTANDING' is FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT from how humans PERCEIVE things (despite very high AVERAGE performance on NORMAL data) — for HIGH-SAFETY applications, this is a SERIOUS RISK (e.g. a traffic SIGN with a small STICKER could cause a self-driving car to MISCLASSIFY it), requiring SPECIALIZED defense techniques (Adversarial Training, robustness testing).
key_points: A neural network learns an extremely complex decision boundary in high-dimensional space; though it correctly classifies most natural data, the boundary can be very close to some points along specific directions with no intuitive meaning to humans

An attacker computes a tiny perturbation (using the model's gradient) along that exact direction to push a point across the boundary, imperceptible to humans — a serious risk for high-safety applications (e.g. a sticker fooling a self-driving car), requiring Adversarial Training/robustness testing

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing the Tradeoff Between Knowledge Distillation and Accuracy for Deployment on Resource-Constrained Devices
question: The Knowledge Distillation technique trains a smaller 'STUDENT' model to 'IMITATE' a larger, already-trained 'TEACHER' model — analyze WHY training the student model to MATCH the teacher's 'SOFT' output PROBABILITY distribution (soft labels) is usually MORE EFFECTIVE than training DIRECTLY on the original 'HARD' labels.
reference_answer: A 'HARD' label ONLY indicates the SINGLE correct class (e.g. [0, 1, 0]) — a 'SOFT' label from the teacher model (e.g. [0.05, 0.90, 0.05]) contains ADDITIONAL INFORMATION about the RELATIVE RELATIONSHIP between the classes that are NOT the correct one (e.g. the teacher model 'THINKS' a 'DOG' image is 5% similar to a 'WOLF' but ALMOST 0% similar to a 'CAR' — this is EXTRA information that a hard label does NOT have) — this 'DARK KNOWLEDGE' (small probabilities on WRONG classes) REFLECTS what the teacher model has LEARNED about the STRUCTURE/SIMILARITY between CLASSES, helping the STUDENT model (though SMALLER, with fewer PARAMETERS) learn SMOOTHER and MORE GENERAL decision boundaries compared to learning ONLY from HARD labels — allowing the SMALL model to achieve performance CLOSE to the LARGE model, suitable for deployment on RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED devices (phones, IoT).
key_points: A hard label only indicates the single correct class; a soft label from the teacher contains extra information about the relative relationship between wrong classes (e.g. 'dog' 5% similar to 'wolf' but ~0% to 'car') that hard labels lack

This 'dark knowledge' reflects the class structure/similarity the teacher learned, helping the smaller student learn smoother, more general decision boundaries than from hard labels alone — letting a small model approach the large model's performance, suitable for resource-constrained devices

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing the Privacy Challenge When Training AI on Sensitive Data - Federated Learning
question: Federated Learning allows training a SHARED model from data DISTRIBUTED across MANY devices (e.g. users' phones) WITHOUT needing to CENTRALIZE the RAW data on a SINGLE server — analyze the BASIC mechanism and ONE privacy limitation it does NOT FULLY solve.
reference_answer: Federated Learning works in ROUNDS: (1) the CENTRAL server sends the CURRENT model to devices; (2) EACH device trains (updates weights) ON its LOCAL data (data NEVER LEAVES the device); (3) EACH device sends BACK ONLY the WEIGHT UPDATES (NOT the raw data) to the server; (4) the server AGGREGATES (usually by WEIGHTED averaging) the updates to create a NEW model, then REPEATS — IMPORTANT LIMITATION: even though RAW data is not DIRECTLY shared, the WEIGHT UPDATES (gradients) CAN (in some cases) still be 'REVERSE-ENGINEERED' (a model inversion attack) to INFER SENSITIVE information about the LOCAL data that produced that update — so Federated Learning USUALLY needs to be COMBINED with techniques like 'DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY' (ADDING CONTROLLED noise to updates) for a STRONGER privacy guarantee.
key_points: Federated Learning: the server sends the model to devices, each trains on local data (data never leaves the device), sending back only weight updates for the server to aggregate (weighted average) — repeating over many rounds

Limitation: weight updates (gradients) can still be reverse-engineered (model inversion attack) to infer sensitive information about local data — usually needs combining with Differential Privacy (adding controlled noise) for a stronger guarantee

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What question does the 'Symbol Grounding Problem' in Symbolic AI raise about the RELATIONSHIP between the SYMBOLS a system PROCESSES and their TRUE MEANING in the REAL WORLD?
reference_answer: A Symbolic AI system MANIPULATES SYMBOLS (e.g. 'Apple', 'Red') according to FORMAL rules PURELY SYNTACTICALLY (based on the SHAPE/STRUCTURE of the symbol) — the Symbol Grounding Problem asks: HOW do these 'PURELY FORMAL' symbols come to have TRUE 'MEANING' (semantics), connected to REAL objects/concepts in the WORLD, rather than being just 'EMPTY SYMBOLS' LINKED TOGETHER PURELY FORMALLY (similar to looking up a DICTIONARY where EVERY definition points ONLY to OTHER words WITHIN THAT SAME dictionary, NEVER 'TOUCHING' the REAL WORLD outside)? — this is one REASON some researchers argue that TRUE Intelligence (especially 'UNDERSTANDING' in a DEEP sense) may require 'GROUNDING' symbols in DIRECT PERCEPTUAL experience/interaction with the environment (like a robot LEARNING through SENSORS and ACTIONS), rather than ONLY processing ABSTRACT symbols in ISOLATION.
key_points: Symbol Grounding Problem: a Symbolic AI system manipulates symbols by formal rules purely syntactically; the problem asks how these 'empty' symbols get true meaning connected to real objects/concepts in the world

Similar to looking up a dictionary where every definition points only to other words within it, never touching the real world — a reason some argue deep understanding requires grounding symbols in direct perceptual experience/interaction (like a robot learning through sensors and actions)

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing the Transposition Table and Repeated States in Game-Tree Search
question: How does a 'Transposition Table' speed up game-tree search (like Minimax/Alpha-Beta), based on the phenomenon of 'transposition' (the SAME board state being reachable via MULTIPLE DIFFERENT move sequences)?
reference_answer: In many games (like chess), the SAME board state CAN be reached via DIFFERENT move ORDERS (e.g. moving piece A then B, or B then A, may lead to the SAME resulting state) — WITHOUT a detection mechanism, the search tree would COMPLETELY RECOMPUTE the Minimax value of that state EVERY TIME it appears (even though it was ALREADY computed EARLIER in a DIFFERENT branch) — a Transposition Table uses a 'HASH TABLE' (usually based on Zobrist hashing) to STORE the results (computed value, search depth USED) of states ALREADY evaluated — when ENCOUNTERING a state ALREADY in the table (with SUFFICIENT or GREATER search depth than CURRENTLY required), the algorithm can REUSE the STORED result instead of RECOMPUTING FROM SCRATCH — SAVING SIGNIFICANT computation time, PARTICULARLY effective in games with MANY ways to 'TRANSPOSE' to the SAME state.
key_points: The same board state can be reached via different move orders (transposition); without detection, the search tree recomputes the Minimax value of that state every time it appears even though it was already computed in a different branch

A Transposition Table uses a hash table (e.g. Zobrist hashing) storing results of already-evaluated states; encountering a stored state (with sufficient depth), it reuses the result instead of recomputing — saving significant time, especially effective with many transpositions to the same state

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing the Complexity of Exact Inference in Bayesian Networks (NP-hard) and the Motivation for Approximate Inference
question: EXACT inference in a GENERAL Bayesian Network (computing the probability of ONE variable given other observed variables) has been PROVEN to be NP-HARD in the GENERAL case — analyze the intuitive REASON for this difficulty, and why APPROXIMATE inference methods (like Monte Carlo Sampling) become NECESSARY in PRACTICE.
reference_answer: EXACT inference (e.g. via the 'Variable Elimination' algorithm) BASICALLY requires SUMMING (or MARGINALIZING) over ALL possible COMBINATIONS of values of the 'HIDDEN' (unobserved) variables — for a network with a 'TANGLED' STRUCTURE (many OVERLAPPING variable connections, HIGH 'treewidth'), the number of combinations to consider GROWS EXPONENTIALLY with the number of RELATED variables — in the WORST CASE (a very DENSE network), this becomes COMPUTATIONALLY 'INFEASIBLE' for REAL LARGE networks — therefore, APPROXIMATE methods like 'MONTE CARLO SAMPLING' (e.g. Gibbs Sampling — REPEATEDLY sampling EACH variable based on its CONDITIONAL distribution given the OTHER variables, then ESTIMATING the DESIRED probability from the FREQUENCY of samples) become the PRACTICAL choice — TRADEOFF: NOT guaranteeing an ABSOLUTELY EXACT result, but able to achieve a 'GOOD ENOUGH' estimate within an ACCEPTABLE amount of TIME for LARGE networks where exact inference is NOT feasible.
key_points: Exact inference (e.g. Variable Elimination) requires summing over all combinations of hidden variable values; with high-treewidth networks (many overlapping connections), the number of combinations grows exponentially, becoming computationally infeasible for large networks

Approximate methods like Monte Carlo Sampling (e.g. Gibbs Sampling — repeatedly sampling each variable given the others, estimating probability from sample frequency) become the practical choice: not exact but good enough within acceptable time for large networks

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing the Self-Attention Mechanism and Why It Parallelizes Better Than RNN
question: At a CONCEPTUAL level, analyze the Self-Attention mechanism in the Transformer architecture, and why it allows SIGNIFICANTLY BETTER PARALLELIZATION of computation compared to an RNN (Recurrent Neural Network) when processing a SEQUENCE (a sentence).
reference_answer: An RNN processes a sequence SEQUENTIALLY (it MUST finish computing the hidden state at step t BEFORE it can compute step t+1, since the LATER step DEPENDS DIRECTLY on the RESULT of the PREVIOUS step) — this makes computation IMPOSSIBLE to parallelize ALONG the sequence LENGTH (even with strong parallel hardware like a GPU) — Self-Attention computes the 'RELEVANCE' between EVERY PAIR of positions in the sequence SIMULTANEOUSLY (based on Query-Key-Value MATRIX multiplications for the ENTIRE sequence AT ONCE), with NO SEQUENTIAL DEPENDENCY between computing the representation of ONE position and ANOTHER — this allows FULLY LEVERAGING PARALLEL hardware (GPU/TPU) to COMPUTE SIMULTANEOUSLY for the ENTIRE sequence, SIGNIFICANTLY REDUCING training time on LARGE datasets compared to an RNN (although the THEORETICAL computational complexity of Self-Attention grows QUADRATICALLY with sequence length — O(n²) — compared to the LINEAR O(n) of an RNN, a DIFFERENT tradeoff to consider with VERY LONG sequences).
key_points: An RNN processes a sequence sequentially (must finish step t before t+1 since it depends directly on the previous result), so it cannot be parallelized along sequence length even with a strong GPU

Self-Attention computes relevance between every pair of positions simultaneously (no sequential dependency), fully leveraging parallel hardware and significantly reducing training time — though its theoretical O(n²) complexity versus RNN's O(n) is a different tradeoff for very long sequences

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Analyzing an Ethical Dilemma in Self-Driving Car Decisions (A Variant of the Trolley Problem)
question: In a situation where a self-driving car MUST CHOOSE between two harmful outcomes (e.g.: continuing straight might harm a pedestrian JAYWALKING, or SWERVING might endanger the PASSENGERS in the car) — analyze why DESIGNING an EXPLICIT 'ETHICAL OBJECTIVE FUNCTION' for such situations is a PROFOUND CHALLENGE that goes BEYOND PURE ENGINEERING.
reference_answer: These situations (a variant of the 'TROLLEY PROBLEM' in moral PHILOSOPHY) have NO UNIVERSALLY ACCEPTED answer even within HUMAN moral philosophy itself (schools like UTILITARIANISM, prioritizing MINIMIZING total HARM, can CONFLICT with schools like DEONTOLOGY, which holds that some ACTIONS — like ACTIVELY harming ONE person — are WRONG REGARDLESS of CONSEQUENCES) — ENCODING a SPECIFIC 'RULE' into an AI system requires DESIGNERS to IMPLICITLY 'CHOOSE' ONE SPECIFIC ethical STANCE (which may NOT be WIDELY agreed upon by SOCIETY), and ALSO involves COMPLEX LEGAL/LIABILITY issues (the AI 'DECIDING' WHO must bear the CONSEQUENCE in an UNAVOIDABLE-RISK situation) — this is why many RESEARCHERS believe solving this problem requires the INVOLVEMENT of PHILOSOPHERS, LAWYERS, and SOCIETY, NOT ONLY AI engineers.
key_points: This Trolley Problem variant has no universally accepted answer even in human moral philosophy (Utilitarianism prioritizing minimizing total harm can conflict with Deontology holding some actively harmful actions wrong regardless of consequences)

Encoding a specific rule into AI requires designers to implicitly choose an ethical stance (possibly not widely agreed upon), plus complex legal/liability issues — requiring involvement of philosophy, law, and society, not just AI engineers

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Why a Strong Model Can Still Fail Due to 'Distribution Shift' Between Training and Deployment
question: A medical image recognition model achieves EXCELLENT performance when tested on data from Hospital A (where the training data was collected) but performs POORLY when deployed at Hospital B — DISTINGUISHING this from ordinary Overfitting, analyze this as a 'Distribution Shift' (Domain Shift) phenomenon and why ORDINARY Cross-Validation (on data ONLY from Hospital A) CANNOT detect this problem.
reference_answer: ORDINARY Overfitting is when a model learns the NOISE in a SPECIFIC training set TOO precisely, detectable by comparing Train vs Validation performance FROM THE SAME distribution — 'DISTRIBUTION SHIFT' is a FUNDAMENTALLY DIFFERENT problem: the data DISTRIBUTION at the DEPLOYMENT environment (Hospital B) is TRULY DIFFERENT from the TRAINING data distribution (Hospital A) — e.g. due to DIFFERENT imaging EQUIPMENT (resolution, CONTRAST differences), DIFFERENT imaging PROCEDURES, or DIFFERENT patient POPULATION characteristics between the two hospitals — since Cross-Validation ONLY splits data (Train/Validation) FROM THE SAME source (Hospital A), it CANNOT 'SEE' the DIFFERENCE from Hospital B's distribution (that data has NEVER appeared in the EVALUATION process) — to detect this problem EARLY, evaluation on data from MULTIPLE sources/environments (if available) is needed, or SPECIALIZED Distribution Shift detection techniques at deployment time.
key_points: Ordinary Overfitting is learning noise in a specific training set too precisely, detectable by comparing Train vs Validation from the same distribution; Distribution Shift is fundamentally different: the deployment distribution is truly different from training (e.g. different equipment/procedures/patient population between hospitals)

Cross-Validation only splits data from the same source, so it cannot detect a distribution never seen during evaluation — need evaluation on data from multiple sources/environments or specialized distribution-shift detection at deployment

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Comparing the Encoder-Decoder Architecture and Its Application to Sequence-to-Sequence Problems
question: Analyze the IDEA behind the 'Encoder-Decoder' architecture for SEQUENCE-TO-SEQUENCE problems (e.g. machine translation: a Vietnamese sentence → an English sentence, with DIFFERENT input/output LENGTHS), and ONE LIMITATION of the BASIC Encoder-Decoder architecture (without Attention) that the Attention mechanism solves.
reference_answer: ENCODER: reads the ENTIRE input sequence (the source sentence), COMPRESSING that information into a SINGLE 'CONTEXT' vector of FIXED LENGTH, representing the 'ENTIRE MEANING' of the source sentence. DECODER: takes that context vector as INPUT, GENERATING each word of the OUTPUT sequence (the target sentence) SEQUENTIALLY — this architecture HANDLES input/output of DIFFERENT LENGTHS (unlike models requiring a FIXED length) — FUNDAMENTAL LIMITATION: COMPRESSING the ENTIRE meaning of a sentence (which CAN BE VERY LONG) into a SINGLE FIXED-LENGTH vector creates an information 'BOTTLENECK' — with a LONG input sentence, this vector STRUGGLES to 'RETAIN' enough important DETAIL, causing translation QUALITY to DEGRADE SIGNIFICANTLY with sentence LENGTH — the ATTENTION mechanism solves this by letting the DECODER, at EACH word-generation step, 'LOOK BACK' and 'ATTEND' with WEIGHTS to ALL positions in the SOURCE sentence (not just relying on a SINGLE pre-compressed CONTEXT vector), handling LONG sentences MUCH MORE EFFECTIVELY.
key_points: The Encoder reads the entire input sequence, compressing it into a fixed-length context vector; the Decoder takes that vector and generates each output word sequentially — handling different input/output lengths

Limitation: compressing a whole sentence's meaning (possibly very long) into one fixed vector creates an information bottleneck, degrading quality with sentence length; Attention solves this by letting the Decoder attend with weights to all source positions at each step, instead of relying on one pre-compressed vector
